Cluster 03 Drill: The Molecular Basis of Cancer, and Stem Cells

H2 Biology 9477 · Book 3 · 9 questions · 166 marks · cumulative over Cluster 1 + Cluster 2 + Cluster 3 + Book 2

Answers sit directly under each part, hidden. Click Show answer only after you have said your full reasoning aloud for that part. Check (a) before you start (b), that is the point of the layout.

Nine questions, and the count comes from the coverage. This cluster owns five learning outcomes, 2(p), 2(q), 2(r), 1(t) and 1(u), and 2(q) splits in two because loss of function and gain in function are different arguments needing separate stems. Six things to carry, plus a potency question and a lineage question the outcomes name by their own examples, comes to nine. Nothing here exists to reach a number.

Every stem is one or two sentences and every answer is long. No stem lists the axes to compare on, no stem tells you which option is wrong, and no stem contains its own answer. Six of the eighteen parts carry the real figure from the paper or chapter it came from, not a redrawing. Two multiple-choice parts only, Q6(a) and Q7(a), both sitting on a figure that does real work, and both requiring all four options to be justified or rejected with the exact feature that kills each wrong one.

Cumulative, so an earlier gap counts double. Q1(a) needs the growth factor receptor, the G protein switch and the phosphorylation cascade from Cluster 1 said cold, plus the whole mutation chain from Book 2. Q2(a) needs the G1/S regulation point from Cluster 2. Q4(b) needs ligand and receptor binding from Cluster 1. Q7(a) and Q8(a) need differential gene expression from Book 2. Q9 needs mitosis giving genetically identical daughters, run backwards. Say the gap out loud when you hit one; the transcript is the gap list.

What the marks reward. Every mutation answer starts at the gene and runs base sequence to amino acid sequence to three-dimensional conformation to protein function, because a scheme rejects the opening marking points where the answer starts at the amino acid and never mentions the DNA. Cancer answers run forwards from the mutation; two examiner comments penalise arguing back from the wild type. The lexicon is strict: allele not gene, long-term self-renewal not divides indefinitely, lymphoid stem cell not blood stem cell or adult stem cell, secondary tumours at distant sites or it is invasion and not metastasis, and rate of division against rate of cell loss rather than excessive or uncontrolled growth.

Two errors in your own chapter are built into this drill, because both sit on distinctions the outcomes exist to test. Chapter 3.4 page 14 calls embryonic stem cells totipotent, claiming each cell of the early blastocyst is capable by itself of developing into a healthy individual. It is wrong; pages 8, 13 and 16 of the same chapter are right. Q6 is built so that believing page 14 gives the wrong answer twice. Chapter 3.4 page 11 says the myeloid progenitor cell can generate all the different types of blood cell. It cannot; it cannot make lymphocytes, and page 20 gets it right. Q7 is built so that believing page 11 gives the wrong answer. 9477 Specimen Paper 3 Question 3 opens on lymphoid stem cells, so that second one is live.

Scope, verified by literal search of the syllabus, and nothing below appears anywhere in this drill. Cyclin, CDK, MPF, telomerase, induced pluripotent stem cells, therapeutic cloning, somatic cell nuclear transfer and karyotype all return zero hits in 9477. 34.8 per cent of the curated stem-cell question bank tests iPSCs, cloning and ethics with no syllabus backing, and the bank was filtered hard before any of it was used here. There is no bioethics anywhere in this drill. Apoptosis also returns zero hits and survives in one narrow place only, inside p53's own mechanism in Q2, because LO 2(q) demands how loss of p53 function gives uncontrolled division and that route runs through it. It is never the subject of a question.

Why so much of this drill is figure-led. Data and figure interpretation is 33.5 per cent of the Book 3 corpus and 35.9 per cent of it is figure, table or micrograph led, rising to 45.9 per cent in the curated bank. Any drill for this Book that is mostly text-only is not modelling the exam.

Question 1 [22 marks]

(a) Figure 1.1 shows part of the H-ras proto-oncogene beside the same part of the H-ras oncogene, with the peptide each encodes.

The cell carrying the lower sequence keeps dividing when no growth factor has bound to any receptor on its surface. Explain how the change shown produces that. [14]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How the change in Figure 1.1 leaves the cell dividing with no growth factor bound. [14]

1. Start at the gene, not at the protein. There is a substitution of a single base in the H-ras gene: the G in the twelfth codon GGC is replaced by T to give GTC. A scheme in this course rejects the opening marking points where an answer states only that an amino acid has changed without the idea that it occurred in the DNA / gene, so name the base and the codon first.

2. Because a base has been replaced rather than added or removed, the reading frame is not shifted and at most one codon and one amino acid change. This is a missense mutation: the codon now codes for valine instead of glycine, so one amino acid in the primary structure of the ras protein is changed and every other residue is untouched.

3. Valine has a much larger, non-polar (hydrophobic) R group than glycine, whose R group is a single hydrogen atom. Both halves of that are needed; naming the two amino acids without their R group properties is half a point. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1]

4. Because the primary structure has changed, the R groups now form different interactions where they sit: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfide bonds form in different places along the chain. The polypeptide therefore folds into a different three-dimensional conformation. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 1]

5. The residue that has changed lies in the binding site of the ras protein, the site that holds the guanine nucleotide, so the altered conformation alters that binding site and hence alters the function of the protein. Where a substitution changes what a protein does, the changed residue is part of the active site or binding site; a residue buried away from it usually gives a neutral mutation with no detectable change in function.

6. What normal ras does, for the contrast. The ras gene encodes a protein belonging to the low-molecular weight G-proteins, which bind guanine nucleotides, GTP and GDP, and work in signal transduction. Activated ras relays signals from a growth factor receptor to a series of protein kinases known as the phosphorylation cascade, and the last protein kinase activates transcription of genes whose products stimulate cell division. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

7. The controlling clause, and this is where the stem's no-growth-factor condition is answered: the pathway is normally activated only when a growth factor binds its receptor. Normal ras is a switch that something else has to press.

8. In the switching step, GTP displaces GDP. Two schemes in this course carry an explicit reject for saying the GDP is phosphorylated to become GTP; nothing is phosphorylated at that step. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

9. The altered conformation means GTP remains bonded as a ras-GTP complex, because the protein can no longer hydrolyse its bound GTP to GDP. The intrinsic GTPase activity that normally shuts the G protein off is lost. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

10. So the protein sits in a constant active state, even in the absence of growth factor, which is a hyperactive ras protein. The switch is jammed on rather than pressed harder.

11. The consequence runs forwards: increased signalling and transcription of the genes whose products stimulate division, so excessive cell division follows with no growth factor bound to any receptor. Write the chain in this order. Two examiner comments in this course penalise answering in the reverse argument, and one scheme records Reject: framing from wild-type.

12. The gene is now an oncogene, produced from a proto-oncogene by a gain in function mutation, and the gene product is hyperactive rather than produced in excess.

13. One copy is sufficient. A mutation of one of the two copies of the proto-oncogene into an oncogene is sufficient to cause abnormal cell proliferation, and the mutation results in the formation of a dominant allele at the level of the cell.

14. The full chain, written out as the marks fall: altered base sequence, altered codon, altered amino acid, altered R-group interactions, altered three-dimensional conformation, GTP retained, constitutive activity, uncontrolled cell division.

R: calling this a frameshift. No base has been added or removed, so the frame cannot shift. R: the GDP is phosphorylated to become GTP. R: starting the answer at glycine to valine with no mention of the base or the gene. R: excessive or uncontrolled cell growth where cell division is meant.

(b) Figure 1.2 shows a second route from a proto-oncogene to an oncogene. In Burkitt's lymphoma the c-myc gene is moved from chromosome 8 to chromosome 14, into a region of highly active transcription, and the c-myc protein is a transcription factor needed for mitosis.

Compare this route with the one in Figure 1.1, and decide which of the two a gel showing the amount and the size of the protein in normal and in cancerous cells could tell apart. [8]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The two routes compared, and which a protein gel could tell apart. [8]

1. The c-myc change is a chromosome mutation, a translocation, in which a whole gene is moved from chromosome 8 to chromosome 14, and chromosomes 8 and 14 are non-homologous. The H-ras change is a gene mutation, the substitution of a single base within the gene. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2]

2. The c-myc translocation does not change the base sequence of the gene, nor the amino acid sequence of its protein. It changes only where the gene sits.

3. The gene has been placed under the control of enhancers or of a more active promoter, so it is over-transcribed and there is overproduction of the c-myc protein. What changes is the amount of protein produced. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Book 2 Cluster 2]

4. The H-ras substitution changes one amino acid and therefore the structure and the function of the protein, while the quantity produced stays the same.

5. Both are gain in function mutations converting a proto-oncogene into an oncogene, and the outcome's own two routes are that the gene product is either over-expressed or a hyperactive protein. This pair is one of each.

6. The judgement. A gel showing amount and size can detect the c-myc route, because the amount of protein in the cancerous cells is greater than in the normal cells.

7. The same gel cannot detect the H-ras route. The mutant ras protein is the same length, since one codon has been swapped for another and no stop codon has been created, and it is produced in the same quantity, so the band appears at the same height and with the same intensity in both lanes. Detecting it needs the base sequence or the activity of the protein, not its amount.

8. Why c-myc over-production drives division at all: the c-myc protein is a transcription factor, and transcription factors are one of the classes of proto-oncogene product, alongside growth factors, growth factor receptors and protein kinases. More of it means a higher rate of transcription of the genes it controls, and hence more mitosis.

The 14-mark and 8-mark totals are [INFERRED, extension, no official key]; the specimen asked 3 and 2. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain, the largest archetype in chapter 3.3 at 34.0 per cent. Trap: three at once. Starting the chain at the amino acid instead of the gene. Saying the GDP is phosphorylated to GTP rather than displaced. And treating every route to an oncogene as a change in the protein's activity, when a translocation changes only how much of it there is. Question 2 [20 marks]

(a) One man has inherited a single mutated copy of the p53 gene in every cell of his body. One woman has acquired, in a single cell of her colon lining, one gain-in-function mutation in one copy of ras.

Decide whose cell is dividing uncontrollably now, and account for the difference. [14]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Whose cell is dividing uncontrollably now, and why. [14]

1. The judgement first: the woman's colon cell is dividing uncontrollably; the man's cells are not. Everything below is the reason.

2. A proto-oncogene is a normal gene that encodes a protein which stimulates normal cell division. A tumour suppressor gene is a normal gene that encodes a protein which inhibits uncontrolled cell division. The school's analogy fixes the direction: the proto-oncogene is the accelerator, the tumour suppressor the brake pedal.

3. A gain in function mutation of a proto-oncogene gives a product that is hyperactive or produced in excess, and a mutation of one of the two copies is sufficient to cause abnormal cell proliferation, because the mutation results in the formation of a dominant allele. The woman's one mutated ras copy is therefore already enough.

4. A loss of function mutation of a tumour suppressor gives a product that is non-functional or absent, and both copies of the tumour suppressor gene must be mutated so that no functional gene product can be produced, because the mutation results in the formation of a recessive allele.

5. The reason both copies are needed: one intact copy still makes sufficient normal gene product to inhibit the cell cycle, so a cell with one working p53 allele is regulated normally. The man's cells each still carry one functional allele.

6. Say allele, not gene, throughout this comparison. A scheme records R: referring to alleles as genes. And a loss of function mutation is at least two mutation events, not one; a scheme records R: referring to loss of function mutation as a single mutation event.

7. What normal p53 does, because 2(q) names it. p53 is critical for its triple involvement in cell cycle control, in apoptosis, and in maintenance of genetic stability, which is why it is called the Guardian of the Genome, and it is mutated in about half of all human cancers.

8. The p53 protein is a transcription factor which binds to DNA to trigger transcription of genes involved in cell cycle inhibition, and high levels are only seen when its DNA is damaged. It is a stress sensor, not a constant brake.

9. Its three mechanisms. It activates DNA repair proteins where DNA has been damaged. It arrests growth at the G1/S regulation point on recognising damage, so the damaged DNA is not replicated and there is time to repair it: activated p53 promotes transcription of the p21 gene, and p21 protein stops the cell cycle by binding proteins involved in cell cycle progression. And it initiates apoptosis if the damage proves irreparable, activating suicide genes so a damaged cell does not proliferate. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 2 for the G1/S regulation point]

10. Run the p53 answer forwards, from the mutation. Where both copies are lost there is no functional p53 protein, so the cell cycle is not inhibited, so cells with damaged DNA are no longer stopped at the checkpoint and continue to divide, so further mutations accumulate and cell division increases. Two examiner comments penalise the reverse route and one scheme records Reject: framing from wild-type.

11. What has actually happened to the woman. One gain-in-function mutation in one copy of ras in one somatic cell gives a hyperactive ras protein, so that cell divides in the absence of growth factors, and it passes the damaged genes on to its daughters, giving a clone of altered cells.

12. What has actually happened to the man. Every cell carries one mutated and one normal p53 allele, so every cell still makes enough functional p53 and no cell has yet lost control. He is one step closer to accumulating the necessary mutations, not further along than that.

13. Uncontrolled is not the same as fast, and this is where the wording is policed. The crucial issue is the rate of cell division against the rate of cell loss: normal tissue holds the two in balance, so no net accumulation occurs, while in cancer division far exceeds loss. Schemes reject excessive or uncontrolled cell growth where cell division is meant, and cell cycle is irregular or inappropriate.

14. The qualification that keeps the judgement honest: one mutation is not enough for cancer. Cancer requires gradual accumulation of several independent mutations in cancer-critical genes, so the woman's cell has begun the process, and describing her as having cancer today would be wrong.

R: referring to alleles as genes. R: referring to loss of function mutation as a single mutation event. R: framing from wild-type, that is, describing what normal p53 does and stopping there. R: excessive / uncontrolled cell growth where division is meant.

(b) Three generations of the man's family have developed cancers in early adulthood, although inside any one cell the mutation he carries behaves as a recessive. Resolve that, and state what has actually been passed down. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Three generations of cancers, from a mutation that is recessive inside a cell. [6]

1. Both statements hold, at different levels, and the answer must name the level for each half. [INFERRED, no scheme in the corpus states the bridge, although the school's own chapter asserts both halves without joining them]

2. At the level of the cell the loss is recessive, because one working allele still makes enough protein, so both copies must be lost before that cell loses control.

3. At the level of the organism the predisposition is inherited as a dominant, because a person who inherits one faulty copy in every cell needs only one further somatic hit rather than two, which sharply raises lifetime risk and brings the cancers forward in age.

4. The second hit is a mutation in the other normal allele, described in the schemes as loss of heterozygosity, and it leads to non-functional p53 protein which is unable to halt the cell cycle, activate DNA repair or induce apoptosis.

5. The mutation is in germline cells, which are involved in the formation of gametes, so it is passed down to the progeny in the process of sexual reproduction; a somatic mutation would not be passed down. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2]

6. What has been passed down, in the outcome's own terms: it is the predisposition to cancer, not the cancer itself, that is inherited. Further mutations coupled with non-genetic factors are still needed.

The two-level resolution in (b) is [INFERRED] and the paired-patient framing is [INFERRED, extension, no official key]. Archetype: compare and distinguish, decided by a judgement. Trap: treating a tumour suppressor mutation as sufficient on its own, which is the commonest error on this outcome, and calling the inherited BRCA-type predisposition either recessive or dominant without naming the level it applies at. Second trap: answering with what normal p53 does and stopping, which two examiner comments penalise by name. LOs: 2(q) loss of function mutation of tumour suppressor genes including p53, and gain in function mutation of proto-oncogenes including ras. Reach-back to 2(o) for the G1/S regulation point and to Book 2 for germline against somatic. Concepts fused: (1) the one-line definition of each gene class; (2) gain in function against loss of function as product activity; (3) one copy against both copies, and why one intact copy suffices; (4) dominant against recessive at the level of the cell; (5) allele against gene as a policed distinction; (6) loss of function as at least two mutation events; (7) p53 as a transcription factor present only on damage; (8) the p21 route to arrest at G1/S; (9) apoptosis where damage is irreparable; (10) forward framing from the mutation; (11) clone formation from one altered somatic cell; (12) uncontrolled defined as rate of division against rate of cell loss; (13) recessive at cell level against dominant at organism level; (14) loss of heterozygosity as the second hit; (15) germline against somatic and what each means for inheritance; (16) predisposition inherited, not the cancer.

Question 3 [18 marks]

(a) Figure 3.1 shows three groups of mice: one group carrying the oncogene c-myc, one carrying the oncogene H-ras, and one carrying both.

With reference to Figure 3.1, account for the differences between the three groups and state what the graph shows about how a cancer arises. [12]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The three groups in Figure 3.1, and what the graph says about how a cancer arises. [12]

1. Quote the data. Schemes in this course state that relevant supporting data must be quoted and mark answers as rejected without the quote, and 13.3 per cent of structured parts in this Book open with a with-reference-to instruction. Give values with units, not the shape alone.

2. The combination of c-myc and H-ras causes tumours earliest and in all of the mice. The percentage without tumours begins to fall at about 20 days, has fallen to 30 per cent by 50 days, and reaches 0 per cent by about 180 days, so every mouse has a tumour.

3. With H-ras alone, tumours appear from about 25 days and the fall is much more gradual, leaving about 43 per cent of the mice tumour-free at 200 days.

4. With c-myc alone, tumours appear latest, at about 65 days, and the fall is slowest, leaving the largest proportion, about 67 per cent, still tumour-free at 200 days.

5. So at every age the percentage without tumours is lowest for the combination and highest for c-myc alone, and the two single-oncogene curves sit between them in the order H-ras then c-myc.

6. The effect of the two together is far greater than the effect of either alone, and greater than the sum of the two: they act synergistically. Note that the combination curve reaches 0 per cent while neither single curve falls below 43 per cent.

7. What that shows about how a cancer arises. Tumourigenesis is a multi-step process characterised by accumulation of mutations in a single cell lineage, and the phrase single cell lineage is where the mark sits.

8. Cancer requires gradual accumulation of several independent mutations in cancer-critical genes, and every step corresponds to one or a few mutations. One mutation is not enough, which is why even the single-oncogene mice mostly stay tumour-free.

9. Each mutation either enhances proliferation or decreases cell death, so the progeny of that cell become the dominant clone, and a larger clone is a larger population at risk of the next mutation. The process accelerates itself, which is why the combination curve falls steeply rather than twice as fast.

10. Both genes here are proto-oncogenes converted to oncogenes by gain in function mutation, so the graph shows accumulation across two hits of the same class; a real human cancer also needs loss of function mutations in both copies of several tumour suppressor genes.

11. Time is the variable on the x-axis, and time is what accumulation costs. A mouse carrying two oncogenes starts two steps along the sequence, so fewer further mutations are needed and they are reached sooner.

12. The honest limit of the reading: the graph shows when tumours appeared, not how many mutations each mouse acquired, so the accumulation model is the explanation the data are consistent with, not something the graph measures directly.

R: describing the trend in words with no values quoted. R: reading the curves as percentage of mice with tumours; the axis is without.

(b) In humans, cancer incidence rises steeply with age, and leukaemias appeared among survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki only five to eight years after 1945. Name the third observation that supports the same model, and state what all three have in common. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The third observation, and what the three have in common. [6]

1. The three lines of evidence for the multi-step model are that incidence of most cancers rises exponentially with age; that there is a delay between carcinogen exposure and the appearance of the cancer, the school's example being that radiation at Hiroshima and Nagasaki caused leukaemias only after 5 to 8 years; and, the one the stem withholds, that cancers develop progressively, from benign tumours to increasingly malignant cells.

2. Expand the third. Benign tumours have few genetic mutations, do not cause serious health problems, and could be completely removed by surgery. Malignant tumours are invasive, impair functions of organs, and mean the individual is considered to have cancer. A tumour passing from one state to the other is a tumour acquiring further mutations.

3. What all three share: each shows that cancer takes time and takes several mutations, because one mutation in one cell is not sufficient.

4. The age observation says so because as a person ages, increased exposure to mutagens such as chemical carcinogens and ionising radiation increases mutations to cancer-related genes, so the mutations have longer to accumulate.

5. The latency observation says so because the carcinogen delivers one step, and further mutations coupled with non-genetic factors are needed before a cancer appears, which takes years.

6. The progression observation says so because it lets you watch the accumulation happening: the same lineage becomes more malignant as more mutations are added, rather than switching from normal to cancerous in one event.

The 12-mark and 6-mark totals are [INFERRED, extension, no official key]; the specimen asked 3. Trap: describing the curves without quoting values, which multiple schemes reject outright. Second trap: reading the y-axis as mice with tumours, which inverts every statement. LOs: 2(r) the development of cancer as a multi-step process that includes accumulation of mutations. Reach-back to 2(q) for the gain-in-function class of both genes shown. Concepts fused: (1) quoting values with units off a graph; (2) ranking three curves at a stated age; (3) synergy against additivity; (4) accumulation of mutations in a single cell lineage; (5) every step corresponds to one or a few mutations; (6) each mutation enhances proliferation or decreases cell death; (7) the dominant clone as a larger population at risk of the next mutation; (8) both named genes as proto-oncogenes, and what a human cancer additionally needs from tumour suppressors; (9) time as the cost of accumulation; (10) the limit of what the data can show; (11) the three lines of evidence, one of them withheld by the stem; (12) benign against malignant on the outcome's own axes.

Question 4 [20 marks]

(a) One tumour in the breast stops enlarging at about 1 mm across and is removed whole by surgery. In the same breast a second tumour reaches 4 cm, and two years later cells carrying its mutations are growing in the liver.

Using Figure 4.1, account for the difference between the two tumours. [14]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Why one tumour stops at 1 mm and the other reaches the liver. [14]

1. The first tumour is benign and the second malignant. Benign tumours have few genetic mutations, do not cause serious health problems, and could be completely removed by surgery, which is what happened to the first. Malignant tumours are invasive and impair functions of organs, and the individual is considered to have cancer, so systemic treatment is needed alongside surgery.

2. Why a tumour cannot grow past about a millimetre without help. A tumour proliferating faster than the tissue around it requires more nutrients and oxygen and produces more toxic waste products that must be removed, and diffusion alone cannot supply a mass beyond that size.

3. Angiogenesis is the process by which new blood vessels are formed. It is tightly regulated and normally occurs only when necessary, such as during growth or repair.

4. The second tumour stimulates the formation of new blood vessels, a process also called vascularisation, and Figure 4.1 shows this directly as new blood vessels stimulated to grow to supply cancer cells with a blood supply.

5. The mechanism is a balance, not a switch. Cancer cells produce angiogenesis-activating proteins, the two named being vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF), and these must overcome the effects of angiogenesis inhibitors. A finely tuned balance between the activating proteins and the inhibitors determines whether a tumour will induce the growth of new blood vessels. Naming VEGF and FGF is description; the balance sentence is the explanation, and it is what the first tumour has failed to tip.

6. The new vessels do two things. They supply nutrients and oxygen and remove toxic waste products, which is what lets the second tumour reach 4 cm. And they provide the pathways for cancer cells to spread to other sites. Metastasis is downstream of angiogenesis, not parallel to it.

7. Separate the two abilities the second tumour has acquired. Invasion is direct migration and penetration into neighbouring tissues, which Figure 4.1 labels as cancer cells invade into local tissue.

8. Metastasis is the ability to enter the circulatory system and travel to distant sites, forming secondary tumours called metastases that are not physically connected to the primary tumour. Invasion moves a cell next door; metastasis moves it to another organ.

9. The three-step cascade, which is what the liver deposit records. Cancer cells invade surrounding tissues and penetrate the walls of lymphatic and blood vessels, gaining access to the bloodstream. They are transported by the circulatory system throughout the body. They then leave the bloodstream and enter particular organs, where they establish secondary tumours at distant sites.

10. The liver growth is therefore a secondary tumour, and its cells carry the mutations of the breast tumour, which is how it is known to be a metastasis rather than a second primary.

11. A scheme records an answer as rejected if there is no reference to secondary sites or tumours. Stopping at cells breaking through a vessel wall describes invasion, and it is marked as invasion.

12. What the second tumour has additionally lost. Tumour suppressor proteins maintain cell adhesion, since metastasis suppressors hold cell-to-cell adhesion and anchorage to the extracellular matrix, so losing them lets cells break off from the primary tumour, as Figure 4.1 labels. This is why losing a tumour suppressor can make a tumour invasive rather than merely fast.

13. The same cells have also escaped anchorage dependence, since normal cells must contact a substratum before they proliferate while cancer cells proliferate in suspension, which is what survival in the bloodstream requires.

14. So the difference is an accumulation of further mutations in the second lineage: enough to tip the angiogenic balance, and enough to lose adhesion and anchorage dependence. The first tumour stopped because it acquired neither.

R: no reference to secondary sites or tumours, which makes the answer an invasion answer. R: treating angiogenesis and metastasis as parallel events rather than the first enabling the second. R: naming VEGF and FGF without the balance against inhibitors.

(b) The patient is given a drug that blocks the receptor for vascular endothelial growth factor on the cells lining her blood vessels. Predict its effect on each of the two tumours, and give one limitation of the treatment. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) A drug blocking the VEGF receptor, and its limitation. [6]

1. VEGF is a ligand and the protein it binds on the endothelial cell is a receptor. Binding depends on the ligand having a specific three-dimensional conformation complementary to the receptor's binding site. Call it a binding site, never an active site, because a receptor is not an enzyme; an examiner comment in this course penalises exactly that error. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

2. With the binding site occupied by the drug, no ligand-receptor complex forms, so the receptor does not undergo the conformational change that would trigger transduction, and no signal is transduced into the endothelial cell. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

3. So the endothelial cells are not stimulated to divide and form new vessels, the balance tips back towards the inhibitors, and the 4 cm tumour is deprived of its supply of nutrients and oxygen and cannot remove toxic waste products, so its growth slows or stops and it may shrink.

4. The 1 mm tumour is unaffected, because it never induced angiogenesis in the first place and is already living within diffusion distance. Blocking a process a tumour was not using changes nothing.

5. First limitation. The cells already established as secondary tumours in the liver are not removed by the drug; it can only restrict their further growth once they too need a blood supply. Metastasis that has already happened cannot be undone by cutting off angiogenesis.

6. Second limitation, either of which earns the mark. Angiogenesis is a normal process occurring during growth or repair, so blocking it impairs wound healing and normal tissue repair. And the tumour may acquire further mutations raising production of other angiogenesis-activating proteins such as FGF, so the balance tips back and the tumour escapes the drug.

Trap: stopping the metastasis answer at cells breaking into a vessel, which is invasion and is marked as invasion. Second trap: calling the receptor's binding site an active site, which an examiner comment records as implying the candidate thought the receptor was an enzyme. LOs: 2(r) angiogenesis and metastasis, both named in the outcome, and benign against malignant. Question 5 [16 marks]

(a) Four people have a raised chance of cancerous growth: a heavy smoker of 30 years, a radiographer repeatedly exposed to X-rays, a kidney transplant patient on long-term immunosuppressant drugs, and a woman who inherited one faulty allele of a tumour suppressor gene.

Explain how each of the four has come to be at risk. [12]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) How each of the four came to be at risk. [12]

1. The outcome names exactly four causative factors: genetic, chemical carcinogens, ionising radiation and loss of immunity. All four are present here, one per person.

2. Write the agent-specific route first in every case, because the route is what turns a description into an explanation. Part (b) asks for the ending they share.

3. Carcinogens are substances that cause or promote the development of cancer, and most cancers develop only after repeated contact with them. Thirty years of smoking is that repeated contact.

The smoker, chemical carcinogens:

4. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in tobacco smoke enter the lungs and spread around the rest of the body via the bloodstream. Reject nicotine, which is not a carcinogen, and reject cigarette and tobacco smoke alone without naming the carcinogen; an examiner comment records candidates losing the mark for exactly that.

5. They bind to DNA to form a physical complex known as an adduct. Unrepaired adducts cause mistakes in DNA synthesis during normal cell division, which introduces mutations. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2, since the mistake is a base substitution in the base sequence of a gene]

6. The link worth quoting: PAHs form adducts at several sites on the p53 gene, so the mutations prevent production of functional p53 protein. Heterocyclic amines (HCAs) in grilled meat work the same way, and nitrosamines, asbestos and benzene instead act directly on cellular DNA, the more potent ones only after being metabolised to a more reactive form.

The radiographer, ionising radiation:

7. X-rays and gamma rays produce free radicals of water, the OH radical, which are chemically very reactive.

8. These interact with cellular DNA to produce double-stranded breaks, giving chromosomal rearrangements and deletions. That is a chromosome mutation rather than a base change, so the route into cancer runs through deletion of a tumour suppressor gene or translocation placing a proto-oncogene under a more active promoter. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2]

9. Keep this separate from ultraviolet radiation, which is not ionising and instead produces thymine dimers, a covalent attachment between adjacent pyrimidines in one strand. The radiographer's hazard is the ionising one.

The transplant patient, loss of immunity:

10. The immune system monitors for and eliminates the vast majority of incipient tumour cells.

11. Suppressed by drugs, or by viruses such as HIV, it becomes unable to detect and destroy cancerous cells through absence or inadequate numbers of immune cells, so tumours may develop.

12. This factor acts on cells that are already mutated. It does not cause the mutation; it removes the surveillance that would have cleared the mutated cell.

The woman, genetic:

13. Inheriting a mutant allele of a tumour-suppressor gene puts her one step closer to accumulating the necessary mutations.

14. It is the predisposition to cancer, not the cancer itself, that is inherited. Further mutations coupled with non-genetic factors are still needed, and inside any one cell the loss remains recessive, so the second allele must still be lost.

R: smoking or cigarette and tobacco smoke without naming PAHs. R: nicotine as the carcinogen. R: giving ultraviolet radiation as an example of ionising radiation.

(b) Identify the one of the four whose risk arises at a different point in the chain from the other three, and give the ending that all four share. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The odd one out, and the ending all four share. [4]

1. The odd one out is the transplant patient, that is, loss of immunity. The other three, chemical carcinogens, ionising radiation and an inherited faulty allele, all act by putting a mutation into a cancer-critical gene, or by supplying one already.

2. Loss of immunity puts no mutation into any gene. It acts later in the chain, on cells that are already mutated, by removing the surveillance that monitors for and eliminates the vast majority of incipient tumour cells, so a cell that would have been destroyed survives and proliferates instead.

3. The shared ending, and this is what turns each description into an explanation. Whatever the agent, the route runs to a mutation in a cancer-critical gene, then uncontrollable cell division, then tumour formation. For all four, cancer follows only from gradual accumulation of several independent mutations in cancer-critical genes in a single cell lineage, including at least one gain in function mutation of a proto-oncogene and loss of function mutations in both copies of tumour suppressor genes.

4. The end state in the outcome's own terms: the cell bypasses the checkpoints of cell division and divides uncontrollably, meaning the rate of cell division exceeds the rate of cell loss, and a tumour forms.

R: saying loss of immunity causes the mutation. R: giving the four agents again instead of the ending they converge on.

Trap: answering with the agent and the outcome but no mechanism between them, which is the difference between describing and explaining. Second trap: putting loss of immunity in the same position in the causal chain as the other three. LOs: 2(p) identify the causative factors, including genetic, chemical carcinogens, ionising radiation and loss of immunity. Reach-back to 2(k) for base substitution against chromosome mutation and to 2(q) for the shared ending. Question 6 [18 marks]

(a) Figure 6.1 shows the first six days after fertilisation in a human.

Which row correctly gives the level of potency of the three cells named? [1]

Aone cell of the 2-cell stage is totipotent, one cell of the inner cell mass is totipotent, a blood stem cell in adult bone marrow is multipotent
Bone cell of the 2-cell stage is totipotent, one cell of the inner cell mass is pluripotent, a blood stem cell in adult bone marrow is multipotent
Cone cell of the 2-cell stage is pluripotent, one cell of the inner cell mass is pluripotent, a blood stem cell in adult bone marrow is multipotent
Done cell of the 2-cell stage is totipotent, one cell of the inner cell mass is pluripotent, a blood stem cell in adult bone marrow is pluripotent

Then justify or reject every row, naming the exact feature that decides each one. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The correct row, and every row justified or rejected. [6]

1. The answer is B. [1]

2. Stem cell potency is the range of cell types to which a stem cell can give rise, determined by the number of possible pathways it can take in its subsequent development. Every row below is decided by asking what a cell of that kind can and cannot produce.

3. Option A is wrong, and it is the row to be most careful about. It calls a cell of the inner cell mass totipotent. Cells of the inner cell mass are the embryonic stem cells, and embryonic stem cells are pluripotent: they give cells developing from all three germ layers, mesoderm, endoderm and ectoderm, but they cannot make the extra-embryonic membranes, so they cannot on their own form an individual. Only the zygote and the first few cells of the dividing embryo, before the blastocyst stage, are totipotent.

4. Option B is correct. A cell of the 2-cell stage is totipotent, since it sits before the blastocyst stage and can produce all cell types that make up an organism, any adult body cell AND any cell of the extra-embryonic membranes, so these cells can form whole organisms. A cell of the inner cell mass is pluripotent, for the reason in point 3. A blood stem cell in adult bone marrow is multipotent, since it gives many cell lines within a specific tissue type, a limited number of cell types, so it makes all the cells of the blood but not other types.

5. Option C is wrong because it demotes the 2-cell stage cell to pluripotent. A cell at that stage is one of the first few cells of the dividing embryo, which the outcome files under totipotency, with zygotic stem cells as its example, and which can still form a whole organism including the membranes.

6. Option D is wrong because it promotes the blood stem cell to pluripotent. A pluripotent cell gives cells of all three germ layers; a blood stem cell is confined to one tissue, so its correct level is multipotent. The precision matters twice over, because a scheme rejects blood stem cell and adult stem cell as not specific enough where a lineage name is wanted.

7. The single feature that decides three of the four rows is the negative half of the definition. Saying a pluripotent cell can become any cell type is both wrong and unmarkable. A pluripotent cell cannot form the extra-embryonic membranes, which is exactly why it cannot on its own form an individual, and that clause is the whole totipotent-against-pluripotent distinction.

(b) One cell taken from a cow embryo at the 2-cell stage and transferred to a surrogate develops into a healthy calf. One cell taken from the inner cell mass of a cow blastocyst and transferred the same way never does, although it survives and divides.

Account for the difference, and state what each cell can and cannot give rise to. [12]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Why the 2-cell blastomere makes a calf and the inner cell mass cell does not. [12]

1. Both cells are unspecialised, having no tissue-specific structures that let them perform specialised functions, and both show long-term self-renewal by mitotic divisions while remaining unspecialised. State the similarity before the difference. A scheme rejects infinite and divides indefinitely where long-term self-renewal is wanted.

2. Both can also give rise to specialised cells by differentiation, so the difference between them is not whether they can differentiate but how wide the range is.

3. The cell from the 2-cell stage is totipotent. It exists before the blastocyst stage, when the cells of the dividing embryo are still capable by themselves of developing into a healthy individual.

4. It can produce all cell types that make up an organism: any adult body cell AND any cell of the extra-embryonic membranes.

5. Those membranes are what a transferred cell needs in order to implant in the uterine wall and be supplied, so a totipotent cell can form a whole organism on its own. That is why the calf develops.

6. The cell from the inner cell mass is pluripotent. The inner cell mass is the source of embryonic stem cells, and in time the inner cell mass will form the embryo.

7. It can produce cells developing from all three germ layers, mesoderm, endoderm and ectoderm, and is therefore capable of developing into all fetal tissues. It is also clonogenic, meaning one embryonic stem cell gives a colony of genetically identical cells.

8. It cannot make the extra-embryonic membranes. That single exclusion is why it cannot on its own form an individual, however many body cells it can make, and it is why the transferred inner cell mass cell survives and divides but never becomes a calf.

9. Note carefully that your chapter 3.4 page 14 says the opposite, calling embryonic stem cells totipotent and claiming each cell of the early blastocyst is capable by itself of developing into a healthy individual. Pages 8, 13 and 16 of the same chapter get it right. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent. This inverts the exact distinction LO 1(t) exists to test.

10. The third level, for completeness, since the outcome lists all three. Multipotency covers lymphoid and myeloid stem cells, which give many cell lines within a specific tissue type, a limited number of cell types, and which exist in adult tissues, above all bone marrow.

11. Where each exists, which is the cleanest way to separate them: totipotent in the zygote and the first few cells, before the blastocyst stage; pluripotent in the inner cell mass of the blastocyst; multipotent in adult tissues.

12. The judgement the stem asks for: the difference is not a difference in genome, since both cells carry the same genes, but a difference in the number of possible pathways still open, which is what potency measures.

R: infinite or divides indefinitely for self-renewal. R: defining pluripotency as the ability to become any cell type, with the negative half missing. R: blood stem cell or adult stem cell where the specific lineage is wanted.

Concepts fused: (1) potency defined as range of cell types and number of possible pathways; (2) totipotency, with the extra-embryonic membranes included; (3) pluripotency, with the three germ layers named; (4) the negative half of pluripotency, and why it prevents forming an individual; (5) multipotency confined to one tissue type; (6) where each level exists in development; (7) the two defining features shared by all three, unspecialised and long-term self-renewal; (8) long-term self-renewal as the required phrase; (9) clonogenicity; (10) same genome, different pathways still open; (11) precision of the lineage name; (12) reading developmental stages off a figure.

Question 7 [18 marks]

(a) Figure 7.1 shows how the blood cells of an adult are produced.

Which statement about the cells in Figure 7.1 is not correct? [1]

AThe common lymphoid progenitor and the common myeloid progenitor are both multipotent.
BThe B cell shown in the lymph nodes carries the same genome as the haematopoietic stem cell it came from.
CThe haematopoietic stem cell can give rise to cells of all three primary germ layers.
DEvery cell shown below the level of the progenitors was produced by mitosis.

Then justify or reject every option, naming the exact feature that decides each one. [5]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The statement that is not correct, and every option justified or rejected. [6]

1. The answer is C. [1]

2. Option A is correct, so it is not the answer. Both progenitors are multipotent: each gives many cell lines within a specific tissue type, a limited number of cell types, all of them blood. The outcome names lymphoid and myeloid stem cells as its own examples of multipotency.

3. Option B is correct, so it is not the answer. Every cell in the hierarchy arose by mitosis from the haematopoietic stem cell, and mitosis produces genetically identical nuclei, so the B cell carries the same genome. What differs is which genes are expressed, not which genes are present. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 2 and Book 2 Cluster 2]

4. Option C is not correct, and is therefore the answer. Cells of all three primary germ layers, mesoderm, endoderm and ectoderm, are the range of a pluripotent cell, and the haematopoietic stem cell is multipotent. It gives all the cells of the blood but not other types.

5. Option D is correct, so it is not the answer. All the blood cells in the adult human originate from multipotent haematopoietic stem cells located in the bone marrow, and stem cells show long-term self-renewal by mitotic divisions; haematopoiesis involves no meiosis at any point.

6. The feature that decides the whole item is the boundary of multipotency. Three of the four statements are true because they respect it; the fourth applies a pluripotent range to a multipotent cell.

(b) Four weeks after chemotherapy a patient's blood contains no neutrophils, no monocytes, almost no platelets and a falling erythrocyte count, while B and T lymphocytes remain at their normal numbers. Her doctor suggests that the haematopoietic stem cell itself has been destroyed.

Identify precisely the cell that has been lost, account for every part of the blood count, and decide whether the count supports the doctor. [12]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Which cell has been lost, and whether the count supports the doctor. [12]

1. The cell lost is the common myeloid progenitor, also written the myeloid stem cell. Name it precisely. A scheme rejects the vague blood stem cell or adult stem cell and demands the precise lineage name, and another states Reject: adult stem cell, as it is not specific enough.

2. The split the answer turns on, learnt as printed: Erythroid and myeloid lineages are derived from the common myeloid progenitor cell. The lymphoid lineage is derived from the common lymphoid progenitor cell.

3. No neutrophils and no monocytes. The myeloid lineage gives rise to the rest of the white blood cells: eosinophils, neutrophils and basophils, collectively known as granulocytes, plus mast cells and monocytes. With the common myeloid progenitor gone, the granulocyte/macrophage progenitor shown in Figure 7.1 is not supplied, so none of these appear.

4. Almost no platelets. Platelets come from megakaryocytes, which arise through the megakaryocyte/erythrocyte progenitor, itself downstream of the common myeloid progenitor. Their function is blood clotting.

5. A falling erythrocyte count. Erythrocytes arise from the erythroblast on the same myeloid side, and they transport oxygen and carbon dioxide. The count falls rather than reaching zero because erythrocytes are long-lived relative to granulocytes, so the existing population is still in circulation and is being lost gradually rather than all at once.

6. Normal B and T lymphocytes. These come from the common lymphoid progenitor, which is on the other branch entirely and has been spared. B lymphocytes make antibodies and develop in the bone marrow; T lymphocytes attack virus-infected cells, foreign cells and cancer cells and develop in the thymus; both function for specific adaptive immune responses.

7. The judgement on the doctor. The count does not support her. If the haematopoietic stem cell itself had been destroyed, every lineage would fail, because all the blood cells in the adult human originate from multipotent haematopoietic stem cells located in the bone marrow. Normal B and T lymphocytes rule that out.

8. The point of principle behind the judgement is that a common myeloid progenitor cannot give rise to lymphocytes. Note that your chapter 3.4 page 11 says a myeloid progenitor can generate all the different types of blood cell. It cannot. Page 20 of the same chapter gets it right.

9. What would have to be true for the doctor to be right: the lymphocyte count would also be falling, and it would fall on the same timescale as the granulocytes, since both are supplied through the same stem cell.

10. The progenitor and the stem cell are not the same kind of cell, and this is worth stating. Though progenitor cells can undergo mitosis, they cannot divide indefinitely, while haematopoietic stem cells can self-renew. A progenitor is partly differentiated, committed to a limited number of pathways of differentiation, and more limited in developmental pathways than a multipotent stem cell. In progenitor cells, some genes coding for proteins to carry out specialised functions are already being expressed.

11. The commitment cascade in full, two lines only: pluripotent stem cell, committed stem cell, progenitor (precursor) cell, differentiated cell.

12. What happens next, and why the patient recovers. The primary role of haematopoietic stem cells is to replace blood cells, and because the stem cell survives it can regenerate the lost progenitor. The numbers of each type are regulated according to physiological need, so the myeloid output is restored towards normal as demand dictates.

R: blood stem cell or adult stem cell where common myeloid progenitor is wanted. R: the ability to differentiate into white blood cells where the specific cell types are wanted. R: naming the haematopoietic stem cell as the lost cell, since the lymphocyte count contradicts it.

The blood-count case is [INFERRED, extension, no official key]. Archetype: data interpretation feeding a deduction, then a judgement on a proposed explanation. Trap: your chapter's page 11, which says the myeloid progenitor generates all blood cell types. The whole question is built so that believing it produces the wrong answer. Second trap: answering blood stem cell or adult stem cell, which two separate schemes reject by name. Question 8 [18 marks]

(a) One bone marrow stem cell transferred into the dermis of the skin survives and divides but is never induced to produce a skin cell, and one skin stem cell transferred into bone marrow is never induced to produce a blood cell. Every cell in that person carries the same genome.

Account for both observations. [12]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Why a transferred stem cell never makes the local cell type. [12]

1. Start from the premise the stem hands you: every cell carries the same genome, so the explanation cannot be that different stem cells have only the genes required for their particular cell line. That option is offered as a distractor on the specimen paper and it is wrong.

2. Differentiation is differential gene expression. During differentiation certain genes become activated and other genes become inactivated in an intricately regulated fashion, so that a differentiated cell develops specific structures and performs certain functions.

3. The mechanism that keeps them inactivated is control of expression, and on the specimen paper the credited route is that genes not required for the differentiation of a particular cell line are methylated. Methylation of the promoter silences the gene without altering the base sequence. [CROSS-BOOK, Book 2 Cluster 2]

4. So the bone marrow stem cell in the dermis still carries the skin genes but has them switched off, and the skin stem cell in the marrow still carries the blood genes with the same result.

5. Commitment is stable, and this is the sentence the question is really testing. Once committed, cells usually do not switch commitment, and in a new environment they will not change the type of cells they generate.

6. That is why the new surroundings do not rescue it. The external signals are present: chemicals secreted by other cells, physical contact with neighbouring cells, and certain molecules in the microenvironment, the microenvironment being nutrients and growth factors in the surrounding fluid. The cell can receive them and still not respond by changing lineage.

7. The signals are received through the machinery of reception and transduction, so a stem cell responds to its niche only within the range its expression state still allows. Self-renewal and differentiation are tightly regulated by the cells and molecules in their immediate environment, the niche that they inhabit. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

8. There is a second, independent reason in the potency itself. A bone marrow stem cell is multipotent, so it gives many cell lines within a specific tissue type, a limited number of cell types, and all the cells of the blood but not other types. A skin cell is outside its range whatever signals arrive.

9. It still divides in its new site because self-renewal and differentiation are separate properties: it retains long-term self-renewal by mitotic divisions while remaining unspecialised, which is exactly what the stem describes it doing.

10. The daughters it does produce are genetically identical to it and to each other, since mitosis produces two genetically identical nuclei, so nothing about dividing in a new site changes what it is. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 2]

11. State the general principle the two observations share: a cell's fate is set by which genes are expressed and silenced, not by where it is and not by which genes it has.

12. The one qualification your chapter itself makes: commitment is stable in the body and reversible in a laboratory. Write the version tested here, that in the body commitment does not switch.

R: different stem cells have only the genes required for their particular cell line. R: answering that the environment lacks the right signals, when the stem states the cell is in skin.

(b) Give the normal function of embryonic stem cells and of blood stem cells in a living organism, and the two examples that show blood cell production is matched to what the body needs. [6]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) The normal functions, and the two demand examples. [6]

1. The outcome says normal functions and in a living organism. Both words are deliberate, so transplantation and therapy score nothing here however well written.

2. Embryonic stem cells: their normal function is to build the body. They come from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst, and in time the inner cell mass will form the embryo.

3. Being pluripotent, they give rise to all three primary germ layers, mesoderm, endoderm and ectoderm, and hence to every tissue, and they are capable of developing into all fetal tissues. Each layer retains stem cells as the organism develops.

4. Blood stem cells: the primary role of haematopoietic stem cells is to replace blood cells. Blood cells are short-lived, so the population replaces them continuously throughout life, dividing by mitosis and differentiating down the lymphoid and myeloid lineages.

5. The demand examples, and the outcome expects them scaled: the numbers of each type are regulated according to physiological need. Loss of blood results in an increase in red blood cell production.

6. And infection leads to an increase in lymphocytes and other white blood cells.

R: stem cell therapy, transplantation or treating leukaemia as an answer to normal functions. R: infinite or divides indefinitely for self-renewal.

Question 9 [16 marks]

(a) Bone marrow supplies new blood cells for a whole lifetime without its stem cell population running out. Account for that. [8]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Why the stem cell population is not exhausted. [8]

1. Stem cells divide by mitosis, and there are two kinds of division to name. Symmetric division produces two genetically identical cells, identical to each other and to the parental cell.

2. Asymmetric division produces one stem cell and one progenitor cell with limited self-renewal potential. One daughter therefore remains a stem cell while the other goes on to differentiate.

3. Asymmetric division is preceded by localisation of regulatory molecules or differential segregation of cell membrane proteins, so the two daughters differ from birth and have different fates. The asymmetry is set up before the division, not decided afterwards.

4. The significance line, which is the clean two-mark answer to the first half: mitotic division of stem cells preserves a population of undifferentiated cells while steadily producing a stream of differentiating cells. That is why a tissue can supply new cells for a lifetime without exhausting its stem cells.

5. The property that makes it possible is long-term self-renewal: the daughters that stay stem cells continue to be unspecialised, like the parent stem cells, and the population shows long-term self-renewal by mitotic divisions. A scheme rejects infinite and divides indefinitely, because the biology is about remaining unspecialised while dividing, not about a division count.

6. Which of the two divisions happens is decided by the niche. Self-renewal and differentiation are tightly regulated by the cells and molecules in their immediate environment, the niche that they inhabit, and in haematopoiesis the niche is provided by the bone marrow stromal cells.

7. Those stromal cells act through secreted signal proteins and haematopoietic growth factors, which maintain stem-cell proliferation. A growth factor is a ligand binding a binding site on a cell surface receptor, causing a conformational change and a signal transduction pathway ending in a change in gene expression. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 1]

8. So the output is matched to demand rather than fixed: the numbers of each type are regulated according to physiological need, which is what a lifetime of variable demand requires.

R: infinite or divides indefinitely for self-renewal. R: describing asymmetric division as the daughters taking different paths after the division, when the asymmetry is set up before it.

(b) A single mutation in one of those same cells can produce a leukaemia. Account for that, and say which property of a stem cell makes both of these possible. [8]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Why one mutation in the same cell can give a leukaemia. [8]

1. The same mitosis that preserves the population also copies the fault. Semi-conservative replication in S phase gives identical daughter DNA molecules, so daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell. Run the genetic-stability chain from Cluster 2 backwards: what guarantees fidelity also guarantees that a mutation is inherited by every descendant. [CROSS-CLUSTER, Cluster 2]

2. So the dividing cell passes on the damaged genes to its daughters, giving a clone of altered cells carrying an unstable genome, and accumulation of mutations occurs in a single cell lineage.

3. Long life is the second half of the problem. A cell that self-renews for the life of the organism is present for decades, so it has far longer to accumulate the several independent mutations in cancer-critical genes that a cancer needs, while a differentiated blood cell dies within days or months and takes its mutations with it.

4. A cell that already divides continuously is also already expressing the machinery for division, so fewer further mutations are needed before division escapes control.

5. What escaping control means, precisely: mutations in the genes that control cell division produce a dysregulation of cellular checkpoints, so the cell divides uncontrollably. That requires at least one gain in function mutation of a proto-oncogene and loss of function mutations in both copies of tumour suppressor genes.

6. Uncontrolled is a statement about two rates, not about speed. The crucial issue is the rate of cell division against the rate of cell loss: normal marrow holds them in balance, so no net accumulation of new cells occurs, while in leukaemia division far exceeds loss. Schemes reject excessive or uncontrolled cell growth where division is meant.

7. The answer to which property does which. Long-term self-renewal by mitotic division is what sustains the pool, and it is also the same property that gives the mutation a lineage to travel down and the time to accumulate more. Asymmetric division is what keeps supply and self-renewal in step, and losing that balance in favour of self-renewal is what fills the marrow with undifferentiated cells.

8. The final judgement worth stating: the two behaviours are not opposites. A tissue that can renew itself for a lifetime is a tissue that must keep a self-renewing lineage alive for a lifetime, and that lineage is the one place a cancer can most easily start.

R: excessive / uncontrolled cell growth where cell division is meant. R: describing leukaemia as the stem cells dividing faster. R: treating the two halves as unrelated, when the same property causes both.
